description_ru: Писательница-призрак пытается превратить скупые воспоминания отставного генерала в книгу. Оказывается, самое интересное он скрывает.
text:
Verity: General Hartley, let us begin with your earliest memory. Close your eyes if it helps.
Hartley: I never close my eyes. It is how one loses things. Earliest memory: a cavalry sword, hanging in my grandfather's hall.
Verity: Lovely. And how did it make you feel?
Hartley: Like a sword. I was four.
Verity: Might we try something more emotional?
Hartley: Miss Lindqvist, I commanded eleven thousand soldiers across three continents. I have emotions as other men have luggage. They are there, but I do not carry them through customs.
Verity: Then perhaps I should tell you what the publisher has in mind. They want a memoir with, and I quote, "intimacy, vulnerability, and a single moment of doubt".
Hartley: I never doubted anything.
Verity: Everyone doubts something, General.
Hartley: I once doubted a sandwich. In Cairo. I was proved right.
Verity: That is wonderful. It is nothing, but it is wonderful. Why do I feel that you are hiding something more interesting behind the sandwich?
Hartley: Because you are paid to feel that. It is what makes you a ghostwriter rather than a typist.
Verity: Touché. Very well. Let me ask something different. In your entire career, was there ever a day you wished you could undo?
Hartley: Ah.
Verity: That sounded like a door opening.
Hartley: It was a chair creaking. I am old, and the furniture is older.
Verity: General.
Hartley: Very well. There was a bridge, in the autumn of 'seventy-four. We were ordered to hold it. I held it. It was a magnificent defence, and it was entirely pointless, because the army we were protecting had retreated that morning, and nobody had thought to tell the rearguard.
Verity: And the men?
Hartley: Eighty-three came home. Forty did not. For years afterwards I would explain to relatives that their sons had died gloriously, and I could not tell if I was lying.
Verity: Why have you never written that down?
Hartley: Because it makes a poor chapter. There is no victory in it. There is merely a bridge, a very long night, and an old fool with a megaphone.
Verity: Or a man who stayed at his post because he had been asked to, and then spent fifty years asking himself who had the right to ask.
Verity: Forgive me, but I think it is the only chapter anyone will remember.
Hartley: You are very sure of yourself, for a person who has never held a bridge.
Verity: I am sure of one thing. The publisher asked for a moment of doubt. You have just had forty.
Hartley: You have a cruel talent, Miss Lindqvist.
Verity: It is merely a talent for listening, General. The cruelty belongs to the rest of the world.
Hartley: That is a monstrous way of putting it.
Verity: It is the honest way. And honesty, General, is the only thing the book has not yet got.
Hartley: Hm. And if I refuse?
Verity: Then I shall write four hundred pages about a sword and a sandwich, and the reviewers will call it "reticent", which is what they say when they mean "dull".
Hartley: You drive a harsh bargain.
Verity: I learned from the best. Shall we begin at the bridge?
Hartley: Let me pour a whisky first. For you as well. It is a long story, and I intend to tell it only once.
Verity: Then I shall write very quickly, and with great care.

questions.question: What is General Hartley's earliest memory?
questions.answer: A cavalry sword in his grandfather's hall.

questions.question: What did the publisher want in the memoir?
questions.answer: A moment of doubt, intimacy and vulnerability.

questions.question: What happened at the bridge?
questions.answer: He held it pointlessly after the army had retreated.

questions.question: How many men did not come home?
